title: SOLID principles in Swift
summary: Five guidelines for code that is easy to change: one job per type, extend without editing, subtypes must behave, small protocols, depend on abstractions.
body: **S - Single Responsibility:** a type should have one reason to change. A view controller that downloads, parses, caches and displays has four. Split into service, parser, cache, view.

**O - Open/Closed:** open for extension, closed for modification. Add a new payment method by adding a new type conforming to `PaymentMethod`, not by adding another `case` to a giant `switch` everywhere.
**L - Liskov Substitution:** a subtype must work wherever the parent type is expected, without surprises. If `ReadOnlyCache: Cache` crashes on `save`, it breaks the contract.
**I - Interface Segregation:** many small protocols beat one huge one. A screen that only reads should depend on `UserReading`, not on a 20-method `UserService`.
**D - Dependency Inversion:** high-level code depends on protocols, not concrete classes. `FeedViewModel` depends on `FeedAPI`, and the app wires in `LiveFeedAPI` or a test fake.
**Pragmatism:** SOLID is a guide, not a law. Over-applying creates too many tiny protocols and indirection. Apply it where code changes often.
keyPoints: SRP: one reason to change. OCP: extend via new types, not edits.
LSP: subtypes honour the contract. ISP: small focused protocols.
DIP: depend on protocols; inject concrete implementations.
Give a concrete iOS example for each when asked.
Balance: avoid abstraction for code that never changes.

code.caption: Open/closed + dependency inversion

mistakes: Creating a protocol for every class with only one implementation and no tests needing it.
followups: **Which principle does a massive view controller break?** Single Responsibility first; usually Dependency Inversion too.
